passage:
Dear Elizabeth,

You asked why I'm walking with a stick at school, so here is the honest version. At the old bus shed on Friday, Karan said I'd never jump from the roof, and the others laughed before I had said a word. I couldn't stand being the boring one, so I said, "Watch me." I remember thinking the laughing would be worse than the jump. It wasn't. I landed badly and twisted my ankle. When the guard's whistle went, everyone ran, and I was the only boy left sitting on the ground. I got the note sent home, and Papa took me to the doctor. Nobody from that group has texted. Uma asked how I was, though. I'm telling you because I'd like to talk it through with someone who doesn't think I'm boring.

Evan

qa.q: Where did Evan take the dare?
qa.a: Evan took the dare at the old bus shed, jumping from the roof.

qa.q: What was Evan feeling when saying 'Watch me,' and what drove it?
qa.a: Evan felt afraid of being called boring; the fear of being laughed at seemed bigger than the danger at that moment.

qa.q: What other approach could Evan have used at the shed, and why?
qa.a: Evan could have joked it off and suggested another activity, or stepped away with Uma, because a substitute lets others save face too.

qa.q: How might Uma have seen the dare and its aftermath?
qa.a: Uma seems concerned rather than mocking, since Uma asked how Evan was, which suggests Uma did not think Evan was boring.

grounding: Worried about being called boring, the student joins a risky dare, the fear of social loss feels bigger than the danger, and the consequences fall on the student alone.

passage: You asked why I did it, Binita Ma'am. I'm Naveen, and honestly? I didn't want to be the boring one. It was after tuition. The others dared me to ride my cycle down the flyover ramp with no hands, and Deepak said, "Naveen won't, he's too boring." In that moment, being called boring felt worse than anything the ramp could do. I knew it was stupid. My stomach knew it. I did it anyway. Halfway down, the front wheel hit a crack. I broke my wrist and scraped my whole arm. The others ran. None of them came to the hospital. My mother did, crying, and she still had to go to work the next day. Six weeks of plaster during exams, and all for three seconds of not being boring.

qa.q: What did the others dare Naveen to do?
qa.a: Ride his cycle down the flyover ramp with no hands.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Deepak called him boring?
qa.a: He felt anxious and stung, as if being seen as boring was worse than the danger, even though his stomach told him it was stupid.

qa.q: What else could Naveen have done in that moment?
qa.a: Laughed it off and cycled home the normal way, or offered a race on flat ground, since a joke about being boring fades but a crash does not.

qa.q: What was that day like for Naveen's mother?
qa.a: She was frightened and upset, crying at the hospital, and still had to go to work the next day.

grounding: A student tells how fear of being called boring led him into a risky cycling dare whose injury fell on him alone.

passage: From my window on the fourth floor I can see the society's water tank and the ladder up its side. It was nearly ten when Mridul and three others gathered below it, laughing, pointing at Zubin. "Go on. Or are you running back to your mummy?" Zubin looked at the ladder for a long time. I can't say what he was thinking. His hands kept going in and out of his pockets. Then he climbed. Near the top his foot missed a rung, and he slid down the last part and landed hard. He didn't get up. The others scattered in about five seconds. I ran down and stayed with him, and sent the watchman to fetch his father. His ankle was badly swollen. The next morning Zubin's father was talking to the society secretary about locking the ladder. Mridul and the others acted as if they'd never been there.

qa.q: What time did the group gather below the tank?
What might Zubin's hands going in and out of his pockets suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt nervous and torn, afraid of the climb but also of being mocked.

qa.q: What could Zubin have done when the taunt came?
qa.a: Walked away and gone home, since a jibe from friends passes, but a fall from the tank ladder could have been far worse.

qa.q: How does the narrator see Mridul and the others afterwards?
qa.a: The narrator sees them run within seconds and then act as if they were never there, leaving Zubin alone with the consequences.

grounding: An observer watches a boy climb a water-tank ladder to avoid being mocked, fall, and bear the consequences alone.
